title: What JVM monitoring tools do you use in production (jstat, jcmd, jmap, Eclipse MAT, VisualVM, async-profiler, Micrometer+Prometheus+Grafana, APM), and which metrics do you alert on (Old Gen %, GC pause p99, GC time ratio, monotonic heap growth)?
shortTitle: What JVM monitoring tools you use in production — jstat, jcmd, jmap, Eclipse MAT, VisualVM, async-profiler, Micrometer+Prometheus+Grafana, APM — and which metrics you alert on

s1_definition.profdef: Production JVM monitoring combines lightweight live-inspection command-line tools (`jstat` for GC and generation statistics, `jcmd` as the modern multi-purpose diagnostic entry point, `jmap` for heap dumps), offline analysis tools (Eclipse Memory Analyzer for heap dumps, VisualVM for interactive inspection, async-profiler for low-overhead CPU and allocation flame graphs), and continuous metrics pipelines (Micrometer exposing JVM metrics to Prometheus, visualized and alerted in Grafana, plus an APM for distributed tracing). The metrics you alert on are old-generation occupancy percentage, GC pause ninety-ninth percentile, the GC-time-to-application-time ratio, and monotonic heap growth that signals a leak.
s1_definition.analogy: Monitoring the JVM is like running a bank's control room. `jstat` and `jcmd` are the live gauges you glance at on the wall. `jmap` takes a full photograph of the vault contents when something looks wrong, and Eclipse MAT is the forensic analyst who studies that photograph. VisualVM is a walk-through inspection, async-profiler is a heat-map of where staff spend their time, and Micrometer with Prometheus and Grafana is the twenty-four-seven dashboard with alarms. You set the alarms on the few numbers that actually predict trouble: how full the long-term vault is, how long the worst cleanups take, how much time is spent cleaning versus serving, and whether memory only ever climbs.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Production JVM monitoring combines lightweight live-inspection command-line tools (`jstat` for GC and generation statistics, `jcmd` as the modern multi-purpose diagnostic entry point, `jmap` for heap dumps), offline analysis tools (Eclipse Memory Analyzer for heap dumps, VisualVM for interactive inspection, async-profiler for low-overhead CPU and allocation flame graphs), and continuous metrics pipelines (Micrometer exposing JVM metrics to Prometheus, visualized and alerted in Grafana, plus an APM for distributed tracing). The metrics you alert on are old-generation occupancy percentage, GC pause ninety-ninth percentile, the GC-time-to-application-time ratio, and monotonic heap growth that signals a leak.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Monitoring the JVM is like running a bank's control room. `jstat` and `jcmd` are the live gauges you glance at on the wall. `jmap` takes a full photograph of the vault contents when something looks wrong, and Eclipse MAT is the forensic analyst who studies that photograph. VisualVM is a walk-through inspection, async-profiler is a heat-map of where staff spend their time, and Micrometer with Prometheus and Grafana is the twenty-four-seven dashboard with alarms. You set the alarms on the few numbers that actually predict trouble: how full the long-term vault is, how long the worst cleanups take, how much time is spent cleaning versus serving, and whether memory only ever climbs.

**One line to remember:** Use jstat and jcmd and jmap to inspect live, MAT and VisualVM and async-profiler to analyze deeply, and Micrometer-Prometheus-Grafana plus an APM to alert continuously on old-gen percentage, GC pause p99, GC time ratio, and monotonic heap growth.

sections.s2_technical:
`jstat` is a lightweight command-line tool that polls GC and generation statistics from a running JVM without attaching a heavy agent. For example `jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000` prints, every second, the percentage utilization of Eden, survivor, old, and Metaspace, plus young and full GC counts and times. It is the first thing I run to see whether old generation is filling and how often full collections occur.

`jcmd` is the modern Swiss-army diagnostic. `jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info` shows heap usage, `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` dumps thread stacks, `jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump <file>` takes a heap dump, `jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary` shows native memory when Native Memory Tracking is enabled, and `jcmd <pid> VM.flags` shows effective flags. It has largely superseded older single-purpose tools.

`jmap` historically took heap dumps and histograms, for example `jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>`. In production I prefer letting `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` capture the dump automatically at the moment of failure, or using `jcmd GC.heap_dump`, because a manual `jmap` on a large live heap can pause the application.

Eclipse Memory Analyzer, or MAT, is the offline forensic tool for heap dumps. It computes retained sizes, finds the biggest memory consumers, runs leak-suspect reports, and shows the dominator tree so you can see which object is keeping a large subgraph alive. This is how you actually diagnose a leak after a dump is captured.

VisualVM is an interactive desktop tool that attaches to a JVM to show live heap, threads, and basic profiling, useful in development and controlled staging. async-profiler is a low-overhead sampling profiler that produces CPU, allocation, and lock flame graphs with minimal impact, safe enough to run briefly in production to find hot methods or allocation hot spots.

For continuous production monitoring, Micrometer is the metrics facade that Spring Boot uses to expose JVM metrics — heap and non-heap usage, GC pause counts and times, thread counts, class loading — which Prometheus scrapes and Grafana visualizes. An Application Performance Monitoring product adds distributed tracing across services, tying a slow request to the specific service, method, and sometimes GC pause that caused it.

The metrics worth alerting on are few and chosen because they predict real trouble. Old-generation occupancy percentage that stays high after full collections indicates the live set is large or growing. GC pause ninety-ninth percentile captures the worst-case stalls that hurt latency service-level objectives. The GC-time ratio, the fraction of wall-clock time spent in GC, flags a JVM thrashing in collection rather than doing work. And monotonic heap growth — the used heap after each full collection trending upward without bound — is the classic signature of a memory leak and is often the single most valuable leak alarm. The senior nuance is to alert on the trend after full GC, not on instantaneous heap usage, because healthy heaps are supposed to fill and be collected; it is the floor that must not keep rising.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's payments service occasionally slows down over several days and then an engineer restarts it to "fix" it, which hides the real problem. This is a classic slow memory leak that only a monotonic-heap-growth alarm catches, so the team needs continuous metrics, not just a restart habit.

Problem 2 — When an incident does occur, the on-call engineer needs to grab a live GC snapshot and a heap dump quickly, then analyze it offline. This is exactly what jstat, jcmd, and MAT provide.

Our mini-project is a runnable self-monitoring service that exposes the exact metrics worth alerting on — old-gen percentage, total GC time, and used heap after collection — and a tiny leak toggle so you can watch the monotonic-growth metric climb. Classes are `MonitoringDemoService` (driver that optionally leaks), `JvmMetricsExporter` (reads memory and GC beans and emits the alertable metrics), and `LeakyCache` (an unbounded cache that simulates the leak).
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
jvm-monitoring-demo/
├── pom.xml
├── run.sh
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/monitor/
            ├── MonitoringDemoService.java   (main + demo classes)
            └── JvmMetricsExporter.java
```

Configuration (what Micrometer/Prometheus would scrape; here, JVM flags for diagnostics):

```bash
# monitoring-flags.conf
-XX:+UseG1GC
-Xms1g -Xmx1g
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/log/dumps
-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags
# Prometheus scrape target (Spring Boot Actuator): /actuator/prometheus
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build
mvn -q clean package

# Healthy run — used-heap-after-GC floor stays flat
java -XX:+UseG1GC -Xms1g -Xmx1g -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,tags \
     -cp target/jvm-monitoring-demo-1.0.0.jar \
     com.bank.jvm.monitor.MonitoringDemoService

# Leak run — watch the floor climb (the monotonic-growth signal)
java -XX:+UseG1GC -Xms1g -Xmx1g -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
     -cp target/jvm-monitoring-demo-1.0.0.jar \
     com.bank.jvm.monitor.MonitoringDemoService --leak

# Live inspection of ANY running JVM:
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000          # per-second GC/gen utilization
jcmd  <pid> GC.heap_info          # heap summary
jcmd  <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/h.hprof   # take a dump, then open in Eclipse MAT
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the service runs ten cycles; each cycle allocates two hundred thousand short-lived byte arrays, and in leak mode it also stores each one in an unbounded cache.

Step 1. In each cycle the inner loop allocates transient arrays that are meant to die immediately. In healthy mode nothing retains them; in leak mode the `LeakyCache` keeps a reference to every single one, so they can never be collected.

Step 2. The code forces a collection so the demo can read a meaningful "used heap after GC" figure. In healthy mode the collector reclaims nearly all the transient arrays, so the used-heap floor returns to roughly the same low level each cycle.

Step 3. In leak mode the collection cannot reclaim the cached arrays because they are still referenced, so the used-heap floor after GC is higher this cycle than last cycle. That rising floor is the monotonic-growth signal.

Step 4. `JvmMetricsExporter.exportAlertableMetrics` reads the old-generation pool occupancy, the total GC time across all collectors, and the used heap after GC, and logs all three with the cycle number. It raises a warning if old-gen occupancy exceeds eighty percent after a collection.

Step 5. Over the ten cycles the healthy run shows a flat used-heap-after-GC line and stable old-gen percentage, while the leak run shows both climbing, and eventually old-gen crosses eighty percent and the warning fires — exactly the alarm a production monitoring stack would raise.

Step 6. In a real incident the engineer would, at this point, take a heap dump with jcmd, open it in Eclipse MAT, follow the dominator tree, and find the `LeakyCache` holding the whole retained subgraph — turning the alarm into a root cause.

```

Oct 25, 2026 1:54:00 AM com.bank.jvm.monitor.JvmMetricsExporter exportAlertableMetrics
INFO: cycle=0 | oldGen=14.2% | totalGcMs=22 | usedHeapAfterGC=61MB
Oct 25, 2026 1:54:01 AM com.bank.jvm.monitor.JvmMetricsExporter exportAlertableMetrics
INFO: cycle=3 | oldGen=47.8% | totalGcMs=71 | usedHeapAfterGC=214MB
Oct 25, 2026 1:54:02 AM com.bank.jvm.monitor.JvmMetricsExporter exportAlertableMetrics
INFO: cycle=7 | oldGen=83.5% | totalGcMs=140 | usedHeapAfterGC=503MB
Oct 25, 2026 1:54:02 AM com.bank.jvm.monitor.JvmMetricsExporter exportAlertableMetrics

  [LEAK: floor rising]  ──refs retained──────→ climbs → oldGen>80% → ALERT

  1. main(--leak) → loop cycles 0..9
  2.   inner loop new byte[256] ×200k
  3.   if leak → cache.remember(...)   → retained forever
  4.   System.gc()                     → reclaim or not
  5.   exporter.exportAlertableMetrics → oldGen%, GC time, used-after-GC
  6.   oldGen > 80% → log.warning ALERT
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
I think about JVM monitoring in three layers. The first is live inspection with lightweight command-line tools: jstat for per-second GC and generation utilization, jcmd as the modern multi-purpose diagnostic for heap info, thread dumps, heap dumps, native memory, and effective flags, and jmap historically for dumps though in production I prefer the automatic heap-dump-on-out-of-memory flag or jcmd's heap_dump because a manual jmap on a large live heap can pause the application. The second layer is deep offline analysis: Eclipse Memory Analyzer for heap dumps, where the dominator tree and leak-suspect report let me find which object is retaining a large subgraph; VisualVM for interactive inspection in staging; and async-profiler for low-overhead CPU and allocation flame graphs that are safe to run briefly in production. The third layer is continuous metrics: Micrometer exposing JVM metrics that Prometheus scrapes, Grafana dashboards and alerts on top, and an APM for distributed tracing that ties a slow request back to the exact service, method, and sometimes GC pause.

The metrics I actually alert on are deliberately few because they predict real trouble. I alert on old-generation occupancy that stays high after a full collection, because that means the live set is large or growing. I alert on the GC pause ninety-ninth percentile because that is the worst-case stall that breaks latency objectives. I alert on the GC-time ratio, the fraction of wall-clock time spent collecting, because a high ratio means the JVM is thrashing in GC instead of doing work. And most importantly I alert on monotonic heap growth — the used heap after each full collection trending upward without bound — because that is the classic signature of a memory leak. The key subtlety is to watch the floor after full GC, not the instantaneous usage, since healthy heaps are supposed to fill and be collected; it is the floor that must never keep rising.

At National Bank of India a payments service used to slow down over several days until someone restarted it, which masked a slow leak. We added the monotonic-growth and old-gen-after-GC alerts to Grafana, and the next time the floor started climbing we grabbed a heap dump with jcmd, opened it in Eclipse MAT, followed the dominator tree, and found an unbounded cache holding every processed transaction. We fixed the eviction, the floor went flat, and we stopped restarting blindly. That is the workflow I bring: continuous alarms on the few leading indicators, then the live and offline tools to turn an alarm into a root cause.
